claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: A musical phrase is a relatively complete thought directed toward a goal, and a cadence is a harmonic event that can mark its ending.
A sentence is a phrase archetype with a presentation followed by a continuation.
A period combines an antecedent phrase with a consequent phrase.
The antecedent normally ends with a weaker cadence than the consequent.
Cadential closure is a common phrase goal in tonal classical music, but other musical styles can establish different goals.
attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

artifact.df: A relatively complete musical thought aimed toward a goal.
artifact.eg: In a short class listening example, one melody line can sound like it reaches a goal even before the next idea begins.
artifact.mi: Any ending pause must be a phrase.
artifact.cx: A pause may happen inside a phrase; the phrase is the whole directed thought, while a cadence is the event that can mark its ending.

artifact.df: A harmonic event that can mark its ending of a musical phrase.
artifact.eg: A cadence in a piece of classical music.
artifact.cx: A sustained modulation is a change of tonic, whereas a cadence is a specific harmonic event marking a phrase end.

claims: Musical texture describes the density of a passage and the way its simultaneous voices or layers interact.
Monophony presents one melodic line without an independent accompaniment.
Heterophony presents simultaneous variants of essentially the same melody.
Homophony coordinates multiple voices at a shared harmonic pace, often as melody with accompaniment.
Polyphony combines voices that carry independent melodic lines and rhythms.
attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

artifact.df: Describes how many independent melodic lines are present at once.
artifact.eg: A solo singer accompanied by a simple piano chord.
artifact.mi: Believing density only relates to the volume of the sound.
artifact.cx: Density relates to the number of simultaneous voices or layers interacting.

artifact.df: The density of a passage and how its simultaneous layers interact.
artifact.eg: A class listening exercise that asks whether a passage feels single-lined, chordal, or independently layered.
artifact.mi: Texture is the same as how many instruments are playing.
artifact.cx: The number of instruments can help describe a passage, but texture is about the density and interaction of the voices or layers, not count alone.

claims: Tonicization briefly makes a non-tonic harmony sound like a tonic, while modulation establishes a longer-term change of tonic.
A modulation may introduce the new key directly and abruptly.
A pivot-chord modulation uses a shared chord to make the move between keys more subtle.
Extended tonicization can blur the boundary between a temporary tonic and a full modulation.
The duration and structural stability of the new tonic help distinguish modulation from a momentary tonicization.
attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

artifact.df: A momentary sounding of a key center within a larger harmonic context.
artifact.eg: A brief tonicization in a secondary key.
artifact.mi: A full modulation that establishes a new key center for an extended period.
artifact.cx: The distinction lies in the duration and structural stability of the new tonic.

artifact.df: A brief local event that makes a non-tonic harmony sound temporarily like home.
artifact.eg: A short passage points to V/V as if it were a temporary center, then the music moves on without establishing a new key.
artifact.mi: Any strong cadence must be a full key change.
artifact.cx: Strong local emphasis can still be only temporary; the key has not necessarily changed.

claims: Tonicization briefly makes a non-tonic harmony sound like a tonic, while modulation establishes a longer-term change of tonic.
A modulation may introduce the new key directly and abruptly.
A pivot-chord modulation uses a shared chord to make the move between keys more subtle.
Extended tonicization can blur the boundary between a temporary tonic and a full modulation.
The duration and structural stability of the new tonic help distinguish modulation from a momentary tonicization.
attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

artifact.df: A key change achieved using a shared chord to make the move between keys less distinct.
artifact.mi: A direct and abrupt introduction of a new key.
artifact.cx: A pivot-chord modulation uses a shared chord to make the move between keys more subtle.

artifact.df: A longer-lasting shift that establishes a different tonic as the new key center.
artifact.eg: The music moves into G major and stays structurally stable there for a while.
artifact.mi: If the new key is introduced suddenly, it cannot be a modulation.
artifact.cx: A modulation can be direct and abrupt, or it can be smoothed by a pivot chord.

claims: Musical texture describes the density of a passage and the way its simultaneous voices or layers interact.
Monophony presents one melodic line without an independent accompaniment.
Heterophony presents simultaneous variants of essentially the same melody.
Homophony coordinates multiple voices at a shared harmonic pace, often as melody with accompaniment.
Polyphony combines voices that carry independent melodic lines and rhythms.
attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

artifact.df: A texture in which voices carry independent melodic lines and rhythms.
artifact.eg: Two vocal parts entering with different rhythms and contour instead of simply supporting one melody.
artifact.mi: Any music with more than one instrument is polyphonic.
artifact.cx: Multiple instruments do not automatically make polyphony; the voices must have independent melodic lines and rhythms.

artifact.df: Refers to a single melodic line lacking independent supporting voices.
artifact.eg: A single vocal line sung without instrumental support.
artifact.mi: Assuming all music must have an accompanying part.
artifact.cx: This is the definition of monophony.

claims: Dynamics, articulation, and tempo are distinct performance dimensions: loudness, the attack or connection of notes, and performance speed.
Dynamic markings communicate loudness rather than speed or note length.
A crescendo increases loudness, while a decrescendo or diminuendo decreases it.
Articulation describes how notes connect or separate and how their attacks are emphasized.
Tempo indicates how fast or slowly a composition is performed and may be stated with text or beats per minute.
attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

artifact.df: The performance dimension that controls how loud or soft the music is.
artifact.eg: A score marked mezzo forte followed later by a crescendo asks the performer to increase loudness.
artifact.mi: It means the same thing as tempo.
artifact.cx: Tempo changes speed; dynamics change loudness, so a crescendo is not a speed-up instruction.

artifact.df: Indicates how fast or slowly a composition is performed and may be stated with text or beats per minute.
artifact.eg: A piece marked 'Allegro' is performed quickly.
artifact.cx: Speed is indicated by tempo, not dynamics.

claims: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

artifact.q: If a positive test charge is placed in a region where the electric field is directed toward a specific point, what is the resulting motion of that charge?
op: The charge will accelerate in the direction the field points.
The charge will accelerate opposite the direction the field points.
The charge will remain stationary.
The charge will move perpendicular to the field lines.
artifact.ex: The correct choice is the first option because the direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate (Claim 1). The most plausible misconception is the second option, which incorrectly suggests the charge accelerates opposite the field direction.

artifact.q: A student places a small positive test charge at a point in space and asks which way the electric field points there. Which choice matches the field direction?
op: The direction the test charge would accelerate
The direction the test charge would move only if it were negative
The direction of the nearest wire or surface
The direction of strongest electric potential
artifact.ex: Correct: the electric field points in the direction a positive test charge would accelerate. A common misconception is to treat field direction as the path of any charge, but the source statement ties direction specifically to a positive test charge.

claims: Muscle tissue includes skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle; all are excitable, and contractility lets muscle pull on attachment points and shorten with force.
All three muscle tissue types share excitability.
Skeletal muscle depends on nervous-system signaling to work properly.

artifact.q: Which statement accurately describes muscle tissue function?
op: Skeletal muscle contracts by pulling on attachment points to shorten with force
Cardiac muscle is excitable but does not contract
Smooth muscle relies solely on direct neural transmission for contraction
All muscle types share the same mechanism of contraction
artifact.ex: Skeletal muscle contracts by pulling on attachment points to shorten with force. This mechanism distinguishes it from smooth muscle, which contracts via internal mechanisms.

artifact.q: Which statement about skeletal muscle is supported by the source?
op: It depends on nervous-system signaling to work properly.
It works properly without any nervous-system signaling.
It is controlled directly by the endocrine system.
It is a connective tissue that does not contract.
artifact.ex: Skeletal muscle depends on nervous-system signaling to work properly. It is not described as working independently of nerves.

claims: The skeletal system is made of bones and cartilage and supports the body, enables movement, protects organs, produces blood cells, and stores minerals and fat.
Bone is hard, dense connective tissue that forms most of the adult skeleton.
Bones facilitate movement by providing attachment points for muscles.

artifact.q: What material composition characterizes the majority of the adult skeleton?
op: Cartilage
Hard, dense connective tissue
Soft tissue
Blood cells
artifact.ex: Option 2 is correct because bone is described as hard, dense connective tissue forming most of the adult skeleton. Option 1 is a different tissue type, Option 3 is not a primary skeletal component, and Option 4 is a cell type produced by the system.

artifact.q: A student says cartilage is the main hard tissue that forms most of the adult skeleton. Which correction is best supported?
op: Bone is the hard, dense connective tissue that forms most of the adult skeleton.
Cartilage is the tissue that forms most adult bone.
Bone is a soft epithelial tissue used for protection.
The skeletal system contains only bones, not cartilage.
artifact.ex: Bone, not cartilage, is identified as the hard, dense connective tissue that makes up most of the adult skeleton. This rules out the common mix-up of treating cartilage as the principal hard framework while still preserving the source’s statement that cartilage is part of the skeletal system.
